Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) end the whole script instead of producing `null`. The script has no filesystem, network, timer, or Node.js APIs; the agents do the work.

Run representative parameter sets, not just defaults.

Check finite vertices and reject tiny-volume debris. Split via `parts=m.split(only_watertight=False)`, assert `len(parts)==expected_components` (set explicitly). A print-in-place “one-piece” assembly often correctly has N disconnected, individually watertight bodies; it need not be one connected triangle shell. Conversely, unexpected one-component fusion means joints got closed, while extra components are debris. Treat `--split` or slicer object count as corroboration, not a substitute for expected count.

3) Joint clearance: label/export each intended moving link separately (or add debug/test export module); compare expected neighboring link pairs, not arbitrary whole-body closest distances. For each pair obtain mesh-to-mesh minimum gap and penetration, compare to per-joint limits: no intersections; nominal clearance within CAD tolerance; minimum printable clearance > chosen validated printer/process threshold (often roughly 0.3–0.5 mm for FDM, tune to nozzle/material/profile). A trimesh sampled-vertex/proximity query is only an approximation/upper bound and can miss closest points in triangle interiors; use a triangle-aware distance backend (e.g. FCL if installed) or CAD Boolean/offset clearance tests for acceptance. Also check shaft/bore diametral clearance and axial end gaps independently. Include as-built tolerances, not merely the nominal SCAD variable. Inspect sliced layers at joints: slicer may close a geometrically valid sub-nozzle gap.

4) Supports/overhangs: process with the exact intended Prusa profile and orientation, first supports off then auto/build-plate supports on, e.g. `prusa-slicer --load printer.ini --load print.ini --export-gcode --output /tmp/no-support.gcode /tmp/assembly.stl`, then equivalent with support enabled in profile/CLI (verify option names with `prusa-slicer --help-fff`; known settings include `support_material`, `support_material_auto`, `support_material_buildplate_only`). `--info` gives input model stats but does NOT prove overhang/support correctness. Parse G-code comments (`;TYPE:Support material`, support interface; exact spelling version-dependent) and count/locate support extrusion; acceptance should usually require zero supports in moving clearances and no support trapped between links. Review layer previews/G-code around overhangs; compare support-on/off outputs. An overhang angle rule alone is insufficient because orientation/bridges matter; G-code is the useful test. Ensure sliced object still has same expected part count, no repair warning, and gaps survive slicing.

5) JSON metadata: require valid JSON (`python3 -m json.tool metadata.json >/dev/null`) plus schema checks for schema version, units='mm', model/source hash + parameter set, intended bounds, expected component count, joint nominal/min clearance and tolerance, nozzle/layer height/material/profile, intended orientation/support policy, and tool versions. Cross-check metadata bounds against trimesh-exported bounds and component count against STL; fail missing/NaN/nonpositive tolerances or inconsistent units. Metadata should be a sidecar generated from the same parameter/config inputs (not hand-maintained); SCAD `echo` text is not itself valid JSON unless explicitly serialized/parsed. Add exact expected values once the design/profile is known.

No files existed to run these checks against. Tool check confirmed OpenSCAD 2021.01, trimesh 5.1.1, PrusaSlicer 2.7.2; note `prusa-slicer --version` is unsupported (plain executable prints version/usage)."}
